text:
Dear City Council Members Jimenez, Doan, Kamei, Torres, and Batra:
I am writing today regarding item (d)3 on the October 17 agenda for the Public Safety, Finance, and Strategic Support
Committee (PSFSS), Options for Expanding Alternative Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service.
Parents Helping Parents is the lead agency in Santa Clara County supporting parents of children with disabilities; each
year over 6,000 county residents are served by PHP.
We ask members of PSFSS to defer accepting the report and direct staff to return within 60 days with updated
recommendations for additional alternative response options to explore TRUST responses to the disability community
beyond mental health disabilities.
Our concern is around Finding #1 and FInding #3:
Finding #1: Finding #1 preference for alternative response The first finding, that members of disabled communities and
their representatives, prefer alternative response programs over co-response programs (with law enforcement), is the
key finding, and all decisions made by city officials should follow from it.
Finding #3: As the staff report details, “Many community members and advocates also supported prioritizing further
investment and resources in alternative response and community-based programs over co-response programs, as
alternative team response can create more equitable outcomes for communities of color and others
disproportionately impacted by the criminal justice system.” (emphasis added). We do agree with the recommendation
to hire more clinicians and others with the skills to communicate with people with particular disabilities, such as those
fluent in American Sign Language.
San José should strive to remove armed officers from as many situations as possible rather than put the onus of safety
on community members, as detailed in several examples from other jurisdictions cited in the staff report.
We would respectfully like to remind committee members that currently 1 in 36 children in our region and our country
are born with autism, and that 20% of the population has disabilities. People of color with disabilities are more at risk
than any other segment of the population when police become involved. In a recent town hall meeting at Parents
Helping Parents, we collected survey responses from families on the top eight public policy priorities for their families: a
full two-thirds of our families of color placed concerns about safety in interactions with public safety staff as one of their
top three concerns for their family.

For our families, these youth and adults with disabilities are our sons, daughters, sisters, and brothers. The TRUST line
staff should be trained and able to safely assist a wider range of disabilities than just those who have mental health
challenges. We ask for a sixty day delay to allow city staff time to meet with and consider the needs of the large and
diverse disability population in San Jose.

item_title: Options for Expanding Alternative Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service. - DEFERRED
text:
To: PSFSS Chair Jimenez, Vice Chair Doan, Vice Mayor Kamei,
Councilmember Batra and Councilmember Torres
From: Showing Up for Racial Justice Santa Clara County
Subject: Item 3: Do NOT accept the “Options for Expanding Alternative
Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service” report
Date: October 17 2024
[name removed], representing hundreds of SJ residents, is writing to
ask that you defer accepting the “Options for Expanding Alternative Response
and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service” report and that you
instead direct city staff to return in 60 days with:
1.
Updated recommendations for additional alternative response options to
explore.
2.
An official, written response from the California Department of Health
Care Services as to the legality of funding TRUST with Opioid Settlement
Funds.
We are thankful for the city’s exploratory investment in a 40 hour/week TRUST
field team as well as its pilot investigation of transferring 911 calls to 988 –
these are a good start and we expect to see expansion of both approaches in
the next budget cycle. And we appreciate the comprehensive analysis that city
staff did last year to identify categories of calls that could be directed to more
appropriate responders than police. It is the response to those findings that
remains inadequate. We also take issue with today’s report in several
important ways.
The report itself found that members of disabled communities and their
representatives prefer alternative response programs over co-response
programs that include law enforcement. Yet the report focuses heavily on
“same old, same old” police responses, like CIT, PERT and MCAT. For
example, the report cheerleads for SJPD’s Crisis Intervention Training (CIT),
even though the California Reporting Project Investigation found that not only
did the introduction of CIT not reduce rates of injury and death for people with
disabilities in encounters, but in fact harm actually increased after CIT was
adopted. Why is a report that is supposed to be about expanding alternative
response spending so many words on CIT, a police-only response, in the first
place?
The report also spends pages reviewing co-response both in our county and
other regions, even though it is a less effective, more expensive and more
harmful approach and even though those most directly harmed by co-response
told the city very clearly that non-police response is the option that will reduce
harm. Furthermore, there are two pending lawsuits in Oregon and Washington
D.C. that argue that police response to behavioral health crises is a violation of
the Americans with Disabilities Act, because it discriminates against people
with invisible disabilities. We send EMTs and paramedics to crises
experienced by people with physical disabilities. We don’t expect police to treat
a broken leg; why would we expect them to treat a mental health crisis?
We do not understand why this report focused so heavily on police and co-
response, when the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services
Administration’s national guidelines for behavioral health crisis
response recommend that mobile crisis teams should incorporate peers but
avoid law enforcement accompaniment (except in special circumstances). Los
Angeles’s groundbreaking expansion of mobile crisis response follows this
model and Chicago recently chose to abandon co-response models. As noted
in the LA report (p. 35), “Co-responder teams have demonstrated over time
to be significantly more costly, while not as effective, as civilian teams that
are comprised of a BH clinician and a peer support specialist.”
The report itself acknowledges that lives are at stake: “Recent national data
indicates that people with serious mental health conditions constitute a
statistically significant percentage of suspects injured in police interaction and
involved in use-of-force cases. For example, a recent national study found that
people with mental health conditions are 11.6 times more likely to experience
police use of force, and 10.7 times more likely to experience police-related
injury than those unaffected by mental health conditions. Mental health
conditions often accompany other disabilities, such as autism, and when
accompanied with other structural social
identities – such as race or socioeconomic status – the compounding
intersection of these conditions and identities can lead to higher rates of
victimization.”
Given that this is the case, the report needs to provide more research on non-
police response models and chart a path forwarding to expanding those
models. We do appreciate the report’s recommendation to continue expansion
of the TRUST program in San Jose. However, we believe that the city attorney
is mistaken about the potential use of opioid settlement funds for expanding the
TRUST program. This summer we met directly with staff from the California
Department of Health Care Services (DHCS) to get a deeper understanding of
how opioid settlement funds can be spent. In that meeting, we learned that
crisis response for substance abuse and behavioral health is typically an
allowable use. However, we don’t expect you to take our word for it, which is
why we are asking for an official, written response from the California
Department of Health Care Services as to the legality of funding TRUST with
Opioid Settlement Funds.
In February, the City Council directed staff to explore the following:
Potential models for alternative response and co-response for incidents
involving individuals with a disability
Alternative response models for welfare checks, disturbances, suspicious
circumstances, and trespassing calls involving mental health issues or
unhoused individuals
Potential models that include partner organizations as a co-response with
police to domestic violence calls
This report largely fails to deliver on those requests. The second bullet point
seems to have been ignored entirely. The first and third bullet points don’t take
seriously the real alternative responses that community members want.
The report also notes that non-police response is a racial justice issue: “Many
community members and advocates also supported prioritizing further
investment and resources in alternative response and community-based
programs over co-response programs, as alternative team response can create
more equitable outcomes for communities of color and others
disproportionately impacted by the criminal justice system.”
We are nearing the end of 2024. In response to the racial justice uprisings of
2020, the San Jose City Council made a commitment and promise to re-
imagine public safety. Dozens of impacted community members met for over a
year to develop over 80 recommendations in the city-funded Re-Imagining
Public Safety process. And four years later, the Council has implemented
almost NONE of those recommendations. Racial justice isn’t a fad. It should
be one of the core goals of a city council in a city as richly diverse as San
Jose. If the promise to re-imagine public safety wasn’t just empty virtue-
signaling, if your commitment to racial justice is strong and ongoing, if you
believe that our city should be safe for ALL its residents and most especially
those vulnerable to police violence, you cannot be satisfied with the report
delivered to you this week.
Sincerely,
The members of Showing Up for [name removed]
sources.

Honorable Mayor and City Council,
RE: Council Agenda1/28/25; File 25-054, Item 2.16

1am writing to support the staff recommendation as well as the memo from Mayor Mahan, and Councilmembers Kamei,
Foley and Cohen. The memo recommends allowing any affordable housing developer to use any bond issuer approved by
the State of California. Currently the city requires the city of San Jose to be the bond issuer.

Over the last 35 years, The Core Companies has developed over 5,000 affordable apartments with the vast majority in the
city of San Jose. Most of our projects rely on tax exempt bonds and recently, many of our projects have relied on recycled
bonds. When not in San Jose, we typically work with bond issuers like CalHFA, CSCDA or CFMA. These organizations
specialize in servicing affordable housing projects and are currently faster, more efficient and more cost effective than
working with the City of San Jose as the issuer. In addition, currently the State program incents affordable developers to
utilize recycled bonds however the city of San Jose is unable to provide recycled bonds. As such, we must work through
an extensive process with staff to pursue an exception to council.

This action will enable an under-staffed Housing Department to focus its resources directly on housing and not on bond
policy or process. In addition, it will enable the Department of Finance to focus the workload of its staff. And finally, it
will help affordable developments in San Jose be more competitive when competing for Tax Exempt bonds and Tax Credits

Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council:

Thank you for voting to conduct a special election for District 3 and for choosing to appoint a new
representative during the interim period. District 3 residents win when democracy wins.

Carl Salas is an excellent candidate for the interim appointment and I hope that you appoint him. I have
known Carl and Marianne Salas for almost 40 years. They are both long-time District 3 residents,
committed to making San Jose better.

They have worked to improve the Campus Community and the greater downtown through volunteer efforts
as well as personal investment. With Carl's energy and Marianne's drive, District 3 will be well served.

Carl has volunteered on many projects, directed clean-ups of Guadalupe River Park and served on the
Guadalupe River Park Conservancy Board. He has led community work through the Rotary. He has high
standards of ethics and has always put others first. His service to the community is unmatched. With his
business experience, community service, his ability to bring people together and his infectious enthusiasm,

Carl will be an excellent interim councilmember

ine Last Thing: The Chi r Mani Majority Rule in the Appointment’

The City Charter is clear that in appointing an interim councilmember, majority rule applies. Section 410 of
Charter unambiguously states:

"If, for any reason, a vacancy, as defined by Charter Section 409, occurs in the office of Mayor or
Council member, the Council shall either fill the vacancy by appointment by a majority of its
remaining members, or call an election for the purpose of filling such vacancy.

This Charter provision confers an important right to the residents of District 3. It prevents a small minority
of the council from blocking the appointment of their councilmember. On November 19th, the Council
voted, contrary to the Charter, to require a two-thirds super-majority for the approval of the interim
councilmember, rather than the majority approval mandated by the Charter. That supermajority vote
grants power to three members of the Council to block the majority appointment of the interim
councilmember.

That rule is contrary to the Charter and is fundamentally undemocratic, giving disproportionate power to
the few and forsaking the approval of a majority.

I appreciate that the motive for this rule was to strive for a consensus pick. But elections of individuals, as
well as the appointment of councilmembers under the Charter, is based on majority rule, not the
empowerment of a council minority.

Please follow the mandate in the Charter and drop the super-majority rule that was recently adopted and
let the majority rule, not the minority. Failure to do so, will cast a cloud on the interim appointment.

Thank you.

[name removed], District 3

item_title: Code Enforcement Operations Study Session
text:
| would like to know what PBCE and DOT staff are empowered to do (or what Council could empower them to
do) when a derelict building on private property is endangering safety along public transportation rights-of-
way such as sidewalks, bike lanes, and transit stops.

This fall, city staff were finally able to re-open the sidewalk adjacent to the burned Lawrence Hotel, on the
north side of E San Fernando St between S 3rd St and S 2nd St. I greatly appreciate that this was able to be
done. What steps needed to be taken in order to get the scaffolding built and the sidewalk re-opened?

The sidewalk had been fenced off for nearly four years. What was the largest source of the long delay, and
what could have been done to allow that to have happened in a period of weeks or months, rather than
years? Is there a new process in place to allow this to happen quicker next time?

What are PBCE and DOT empowered to do (or what could Council empower them to do) to enhance safety
and accessibility along public transportation rights-of-way in situations like this. For example:

* Does the city have authority to perform emergency work on the edge of the private property, with or
without the permission of the property owner, if the property owner is refusing to do such work
themselves in a timely manner? And if the city can do that, can it also sue the private property owner to
recover the expenses of that work?

* Can DOT use temporary materials (eg. cones, plastic posts) to shift/reallocate space within the right-of-
way, allowing pedestrians to have a safe path of travel around the obstruction? For example, can DOT
use cones or plastic posts to temporarily remove some parking or remove/narrow some car travel lanes,
in order to make room to shift the bikeways and "sidewalks"? And can DOT add temporary curb ramps
(like those in San Pedro Square) to allow ADA access in and out of the impromptu walking path?

© Do DOT, Code Enforcement, or SJPD have any enhanced enforcement powers in cases where the public
transportation right-of-way is impeded or endangered by a derelict building?

¢ Is there any action that Council can take to empower city staff in the above ways?

What actions can be taken, and by what department(s), when private property is being stored indefinitely in a
transportation right-of-way? An example that comes to my mind is a business's dumpster that seems to be
stored in a bike lane 24/7/365. Which department is responsible for addressing such an issue, and how
quickly could such an issue be resolved?

Slides 6 indicates which departments are responsible for "Maintenance and Preservation of the Built
Environment" on private vs. public property. But when private property creates a physical impact on public
right-of-way, is there a straightforward, unambiguous, and timely procedure for ensuring that at least one
department is actively working on resolving the incident? Or are there any difficulties with such incidents
falling through the cracks, or bouncing back-and-forth between departments?

Thanks,

[name removed] (speaking on my own behalf)
District 3, Japantown, 95112

RE: Planning, Building, and Code Enforcement (PBCE) Code Enforcement Operations Study
Session
Dear Mayor Mahan and Honorable Councilmembers,
Downtown is not the only San Jose district facing pervasive blight. "What's up with the busted buildings in
Japantown," is a phrase I've been asked far too many times.
In just over two blocks of our Business Improvement District, we have ten boarded-up or vacant
commercial and residential buildings. All but two are listed on the City of San Jose's Historic Resources
Inventory and blighted in part due to restrictive historic mandates. There are over 125 Japantown parcels in
the Historic Resources Inventory, and virtually none of our property owners are aware of it.
Complex dialogue between San Jose's Historic Landmarks Commission, Code Enforcement, Planning, and
Building Departments, as well as unclear distinctions between local and state building regulations for
historic properties compounds the issue.
The term "blighted" has historically been used to designate properties and land for government-backed
seizure under eminent domain and has racist implications. I am using this language in its contemporary
form to call out the results of prohibitive measures that prevented our community from maintaining its
properties.
• Three buildings on Taylor Street have been boarded up for over 2 years and underwent a $25K review
by a City-approved Historic Resources Consultant and multiple checks by the aforementioned City
departments. In that time, thieves have stripped one building entirely of its electrical wires, including the
service panel, and squatters have attempted to set fire to it three times.
• One residential home on N. 5th Street has been vacant and condemned for over 20 years. I have
personally boarded it up twice on behalf of its senior owners.
• Two other residential homes on N. 4th Street stand in the way of a new Dharma Center and preschool
for the Buddhist Church. My great-uncle owned one home and has the family's blessing to be
demolished. It's been boarded up for over 20 years.
• A two-story brick building on N. 6th Street requires more than $1M in seismic retrofitting. It has
changed ownership three times in fifteen years, has been vacant for over twenty, and recently had a
piece of the structure fall from the second story onto the public sidewalk. The interior second floor has
collapsed, and the building has also caught fire. Investors sell the building when they realize it is
financially unsustainable to retrofit.
• The Kawakami House, moved to make room for the Japanese American Museum of San Jose in 2006,
remains boarded up, frequently invaded by squatters, and without the substantial monetary investment
– estimated to be $2.5M – for renovation.
• The Mineta House, the former childhood home of Japantown's own Norman Mineta, has exceeded its
renovation budget as its new owners, one of Japantown's leading churches, discovered that their plans
needed to meet historic requirements.
565 N. 6th Street, Suite G. San Jose, CA 95112. phone [phone removed]. [email removed]
These parcels are not owned by irresponsible offshore entities but almost entirely by local families and
nonprofits. The requirements meant to protect our history are causing the opposite – bankrupting our
families, damaging our nonprofits, and exposing our community to theft, squatters, fire, physical harm, and
vulnerability to corporate gentrification or eminent domain.
As someone who is 5th generation Japantown and whose grandparents and great-grandparents, aunts,
and uncles were incarcerated during WWII, I understand the importance of our own history. Our family also
moved and restored our historic 19th Century Italianate Victorian home and rebuilt our Grandfather's
Japantown gas station as a coffee shop. We fully understand the financial and logistical challenges of
landmark renovation.
We want to preserve our legacy, history, and places, but it's time for the City to allow us the permission,
flexibility, and authority to determine our future. We need help to achieve a reasonable balance between
preservation and growth that strengthens our historically marginalized, ethnic community.
We appreciate any and all consideration the City Council, Code Enforcement, Historic Landmarks
Commission, and Historic Preservation Officer may provide us.
Best,
[name removed]
President, Japantown Business Association
565 N. 6th Street, Suite G. San Jose, CA 95112. phone [phone removed]. [email removed]

text:
Clerk San Jose Councilmember,
Dear Rules Committee Members,
As a resident of San Jose and as a first generation Latine, I am writing to express my strong
support for the memo proposed by Councilmembers Ortiz, Campos, Cohen, and Candelas,
which outlines critical actions to protect our city's residents from the harmful policies of
the incoming presidential administration.
San Jose has always been a city that values its diversity and stands with its immigrant
communities, who are essential to our city. The threats posed by mass deportation policies
and heightened immigration enforcement risk tearing families apart, spreading fear, and
undermining public safety.
The steps outlined in this memo - strengthening the Rapid Response Network, providing
legal and support services, and reaffirming our sanctuary city policies - are vital to
preserving the trust, safety, and dignity of all San Jose residents. By passing this memo, the
City Council can send a clear message that San Jose will remain a place where all
communities are valued and protected.
I urge you to pass this memo to safeguard our city's future.
Thank you for your leadership and commitment to ensuring that San Jose remains a
welcoming and inclusive city for everyone.
Sincerely

Clerk San Jose Councilmember,
Dear Rules Committee Members,

My name is [name removed], and | work in San José, where | am dedicated to supporting our
community, particularly individuals with developmental disabilities. | am writing to express
my strong support for the memo proposed by Councilmembers Ortiz, Campos, Cohen,
and Candelas, which outlines crucial actions to protect our city’s residents from the
harmful policies of the incoming presidential administration.

San José has long been a place of refuge for immigrants seeking safety, stability, and
opportunity. Among those immigrants, many families of individuals with developmental
disabilities rely heavily on the supportive resources our city provides, including housing,
healthcare, and social services. For these families, especially those who are undocumented
or have uncertain immigration status, San José represents more than just a city—it is a
lifeline, offering a place where they can rebuild their lives, access the care they need, and
seek safety and stability for their loved ones.

Housing is a cornerstone of this stability. Families, particularly those navigating the
compounded challenges of disability and immigration status, face immense pressure in
securing housing. Disrupting these families through deportation and immigration
enforcement puts them at even greater risk of homelessness and isolation, leaving

individuals with developmental disabilities without the essential medical and emotional
support systems they need to thrive.

San José is home to a diverse immigrant population, many of whom are in urgent need of
accessible housing and supportive services. We must remain open, kind, and human in our
approach, ensuring that all immigrants, especially those with disabilities or navigating
precarious legal status, feel welcomed and supported in our city. The steps outlined in this
memo—strengthening the Rapid Response Network, providing legal and support services,
and reaffirming our sanctuary city policies—are vital to ensuring these families and
individuals receive the protection and stability they deserve.

| urge you to pass this memo to protect immigrant families and ensure San José continues
to be a city that embodies compassion and inclusion. Your leadership is essential in
preserving the dignity, safety, and stability of our most vulnerable residents, ensuring that
all families, including those with members with developmental disabilities, can thrive in a
secure and supportive environment.

Thank you for your dedication to creating a better future for all who call San José home.

Sincerely,

Re: Including “All” Immigrants in Proclamation (Item 2.9 of February 4th Council Meeting)
As an organization that advocates for immigrant rights, racial justice, and freedom from the carceral
system -- all of which we see as expressions of the same struggle -- we are calling on the City of San
Jose to revise this proclamation.
San Jose must create an inclusive resolution to stand with all immigrants, not only some. As
currently written, and expressed in media statements by the Mayor - the City of San Jose is
acquiescing to Trump’s anti-immigrant agenda by endorsing the detention and deportation of
immigrant community members who have had contact with the criminal legal system.
The excluding language of “law-abiding” in the resolution is intended to message to the community
that San Jose is willing to sacrifice our fellow community members, our neighbors, our loved ones
simply because of their contact with the criminal legal system. It is the ignorant and false dichotomy
of the “good” versus “bad” immigrant - who is deserving of rights and who is not. San Jose should
be a city that sees through that illusionary and racist frame - and protects all our community
members.
This rubber-stamping of who the city is willing to allow ICE to detain is legally incorrect,
strategically naive, and ultimately counter to our city’s collective values of inclusion.
For one, the criminal legal system is not a proxy for immigration enforcement. A city messaging that
if someone has a criminal record, they are not due the same level of solidarity or protection is
unethical - that the city would codify that into a proclamation that is by definition aspirational, is
abhorrent. This thinking, that the rights of some immigrants should be protected while others
abandoned, only bolsters Trump’s racist and false specter of the “dangerous” immigrants. Plus, in
response to the question of who is being targeted in mass deportation campaigns - the
administration clearly stated all undocumented immigrants are “criminals.” Who the city avails
protections to, and who it does not, is a slippery slope that ultimately leaves all immigrant
communities vulnerable.
There is a key word missing from the title of this proclamation. The word is “all” - that the city of
San Jose is reaffirming the city’s commitment to protecting the rights and safety of “all” immigrant
communities.

Dear City Council Members Jimenez, Doan, Kamei, Torres, and Batra:
I am writing today regarding item (d)3 on the October 17 agenda for the Public Safety, Finance, and Strategic Support
Committee (PSFSS), Options for Expanding Alternative Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service.
Parents Helping Parents is the lead agency in Santa Clara County supporting parents of children with disabilities; each
year over 6,000 county residents are served by PHP.
We ask members of PSFSS to defer accepting the report and direct staff to return within 60 days with updated
recommendations for additional alternative response options to explore TRUST responses to the disability community
beyond mental health disabilities.
Our concern is around Finding #1 and FInding #3:
Finding #1: Finding #1 preference for alternative response The first finding, that members of disabled communities and
their representatives, prefer alternative response programs over co-response programs (with law enforcement), is the
key finding, and all decisions made by city officials should follow from it.
Finding #3: As the staff report details, “Many community members and advocates also supported prioritizing further
investment and resources in alternative response and community-based programs over co-response programs, as
alternative team response can create more equitable outcomes for communities of color and others
disproportionately impacted by the criminal justice system.” (emphasis added). We do agree with the recommendation
to hire more clinicians and others with the skills to communicate with people with particular disabilities, such as those
fluent in American Sign Language.
San José should strive to remove armed officers from as many situations as possible rather than put the onus of safety
on community members, as detailed in several examples from other jurisdictions cited in the staff report.
We would respectfully like to remind committee members that currently 1 in 36 children in our region and our country
are born with autism, and that 20% of the population has disabilities. People of color with disabilities are more at risk
than any other segment of the population when police become involved. In a recent town hall meeting at Parents
Helping Parents, we collected survey responses from families on the top eight public policy priorities for their families: a
full two-thirds of our families of color placed concerns about safety in interactions with public safety staff as one of their
top three concerns for their family.

staff should be trained and able to safely assist a wider range of disabilities than just those who have mental health

text:
To: PSFSS Chair Jimenez, Vice Chair Doan, Vice Mayor Kamei,
Councilmember Batra and Councilmember Torres
From: Showing Up for Racial Justice Santa Clara County
Subject: Item 3: Do NOT accept the “Options for Expanding Alternative
Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service” report
Date: October 17 2024
[name removed], representing hundreds of SJ residents, is writing to
ask that you defer accepting the “Options for Expanding Alternative Response
and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service” report and that you
instead direct city staff to return in 60 days with:
1.
Updated recommendations for additional alternative response options to
explore.
2.
An official, written response from the California Department of Health
Care Services as to the legality of funding TRUST with Opioid Settlement
Funds.
We are thankful for the city’s exploratory investment in a 40 hour/week TRUST
field team as well as its pilot investigation of transferring 911 calls to 988 –
these are a good start and we expect to see expansion of both approaches in
the next budget cycle. And we appreciate the comprehensive analysis that city
staff did last year to identify categories of calls that could be directed to more
appropriate responders than police. It is the response to those findings that
remains inadequate. We also take issue with today’s report in several
important ways.
The report itself found that members of disabled communities and their
representatives prefer alternative response programs over co-response
programs that include law enforcement. Yet the report focuses heavily on
“same old, same old” police responses, like CIT, PERT and MCAT. For
example, the report cheerleads for SJPD’s Crisis Intervention Training (CIT),
even though the California Reporting Project Investigation found that not only
did the introduction of CIT not reduce rates of injury and death for people with
disabilities in encounters, but in fact harm actually increased after CIT was
adopted. Why is a report that is supposed to be about expanding alternative
response spending so many words on CIT, a police-only response, in the first
place?
The report also spends pages reviewing co-response both in our county and
other regions, even though it is a less effective, more expensive and more
harmful approach and even though those most directly harmed by co-response
told the city very clearly that non-police response is the option that will reduce
harm. Furthermore, there are two pending lawsuits in Oregon and Washington
D.C. that argue that police response to behavioral health crises is a violation of
the Americans with Disabilities Act, because it discriminates against people
with invisible disabilities. We send EMTs and paramedics to crises
experienced by people with physical disabilities. We don’t expect police to treat
a broken leg; why would we expect them to treat a mental health crisis?
We do not understand why this report focused so heavily on police and co-
response, when the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services
Administration’s national guidelines for behavioral health crisis
response recommend that mobile crisis teams should incorporate peers but
avoid law enforcement accompaniment (except in special circumstances). Los
Angeles’s groundbreaking expansion of mobile crisis response follows this
model and Chicago recently chose to abandon co-response models. As noted
in the LA report (p. 35), “Co-responder teams have demonstrated over time
to be significantly more costly, while not as effective, as civilian teams that
are comprised of a BH clinician and a peer support specialist.”
The report itself acknowledges that lives are at stake: “Recent national data
indicates that people with serious mental health conditions constitute a
statistically significant percentage of suspects injured in police interaction and
involved in use-of-force cases. For example, a recent national study found that
people with mental health conditions are 11.6 times more likely to experience
police use of force, and 10.7 times more likely to experience police-related
injury than those unaffected by mental health conditions. Mental health
conditions often accompany other disabilities, such as autism, and when
accompanied with other structural social
identities – such as race or socioeconomic status – the compounding
intersection of these conditions and identities can lead to higher rates of
victimization.”
Given that this is the case, the report needs to provide more research on non-
police response models and chart a path forwarding to expanding those
models. We do appreciate the report’s recommendation to continue expansion
of the TRUST program in San Jose. However, we believe that the city attorney
is mistaken about the potential use of opioid settlement funds for expanding the
TRUST program. This summer we met directly with staff from the California
Department of Health Care Services (DHCS) to get a deeper understanding of
how opioid settlement funds can be spent. In that meeting, we learned that
crisis response for substance abuse and behavioral health is typically an
allowable use. However, we don’t expect you to take our word for it, which is
why we are asking for an official, written response from the California
Department of Health Care Services as to the legality of funding TRUST with
Opioid Settlement Funds.
In February, the City Council directed staff to explore the following:
Potential models for alternative response and co-response for incidents
involving individuals with a disability
Alternative response models for welfare checks, disturbances, suspicious
circumstances, and trespassing calls involving mental health issues or
unhoused individuals
Potential models that include partner organizations as a co-response with
